Flat at the top line, violent underneath. The book finished the week 0.16% lower than it started, and that number hides two moves in opposite directions. GRPN ran about fifteen per cent higher on Monday, almost all of it intraday, and closed the week at 21.30 — above the 20 strike it is short into October, so the upside was capped at the strike and the rest of the move accrues to whoever bought the call. XNDU went the other way and went at once: twenty per cent of it was gone at Tuesday's open, on fifteen times the previous session's volume, and it kept sliding to 4.98 — off roughly a third on the week, with nothing written against the downside because a covered call does not defend anything. The two roughly cancelled. That is the trade-off in the engine stated plainly: premium sells the upside and buys no protection, and this week both halves of that arrived at once. XNDU now carries the worst mark in the book at better than fifty percent below carry.

Monday put premium back to work. Calls went out on BBAI at 0.30 — the first real premium written on that name after two expiries sold at a cent, which covers the stock on paper and earns nothing — plus HUN at 0.06, XNDU at 0.15, and ACTG at 0.13 once that position was built out on Tuesday. The SERV calls were rolled, and rolled badly: buying the September contracts back cost more than they were sold for, and the replacements went out at two cents, which is the cent-premium fault again. The card now carries both halves of that at the top. The week charged 0.75% of net asset value in written premium and earned −0.11% of it back, which is still the only week on the record where the two point opposite ways: the engine gave back more than it collected, and the SERV roll is the whole of the gap. That earned figure read −0.27% when this card first went out, with the Friday expiries on XNDU and SERV sitting in the feed as processed rows carrying no P&L at all. They booked a week later, restamped Friday 20:20 UTC under new trade ids, worth 0.16% of net asset value between them — the card predicted “roughly 0.16%” and that is the restated figure above. The letter was a C+ on both sets and stays one, which is why this card went out rather than waiting.

The reserve is the real fault of the week. Tuesday spent it: two new names sized in, ACTG and BHF, three existing ones added to below their carry in ACTG, PR and OLN, and SPCX and PLTR topped up above theirs. Cash closed at 0.1% of net asset value — the thinnest reading of the record — against a 2% floor, one week after a strike being hit had lifted the reserve to 8.8%. It took two sessions to spend a month of patience. The book is not levered and is not borrowing: gross exposure is 1.04× and the cash balance is positive. But there is nothing to meet an assignment with, nothing to defend a position with, and no capacity to act on anything that shows up next week. Averaging down three names into an empty reserve is the exact sequence this book is meant to grade against.

Concentration rose with it. SPCX ran to 20.9% of net asset value and PLTR to 20.7%, each up better than two points, and each was added to on the way up rather than trimmed into strength. Neither breaches the 25% band. Both are now larger than anything else in the book, neither carries a written call, and the direction is the wrong one.

The event sleeve ran a third consecutive week on JPUSD, the root the forecast engine bans. Size collapsed to 40 contracts at 0.63, about 0.1% of net asset value, against 700 the week before. That is below the engine's own 100-contract minimum, so the ticket clears neither rule — it is smaller than the sizing rule wants, in a name the ban forbids. It settled Thursday evening and has since booked: all 40 paid, for +0.1% of net asset value on 0.1% staked. Being right about the yen on a ticket that clears neither rule is the outcome the ban is written for, not an argument against it. Last week's does now book. The 700 contracts netted +0.5% of net asset value at a 1.52 profit factor, all seven tickets paying and none settling worthless; the Sep 18 card has been updated to carry the figure, as it said it would.

reports.note:
One name made the week, in one session. The book finished up 1.04%, and it was underwater until Thursday to get there: down 1.67% by Monday's close, still down 0.63% on Wednesday, and only green on Thursday afternoon. Then SPCX gained better than seven per cent on Friday alone, on close to twice its usual volume, and carried the whole week on its own — the position added about one and a half points of net asset value while everything else, netted together, lost ground. Eight of thirteen names finished lower. That is not a week the book earned; it is a week a single holding handed it, and the holding in question is now the largest position on the sheet at 22.2% of net asset value with no call written against it.

GRPN went the other way and ran the engine's trade in reverse. The shares fell about nine per cent to 19.31, back underneath the 20 strike they are short into October, and the call written against them lost roughly two thirds of its mark in the process. The option leg made money while the share leg lost more of it — which is exactly the shape of last week in mirror image, when GRPN ran fifteen per cent into the same strike and the upside was capped. A covered call does not change the direction of a name. It narrows the range of outcomes and charges for doing so, and across two weeks GRPN has now paid out both ends of that range. XNDU kept falling, down another fourteen per cent to 4.30 and now fifty-nine per cent below carry, the worst mark in the book for a second straight week.

Not a single share changed hands all week. The only executions on the securities side were Monday morning's calls: seven contracts on SERV at 0.18 and two on XNDU at 0.08, both out to the October 9 expiry, for 0.49% of net asset value in written premium. The SERV write is the point worth noting — 0.18 against the two-cent replacements that were criticised on this card a week ago, which is the engine being run properly rather than kept nominally alive. Nothing booked as earned this week because nothing expired or was bought back, so the earned line reads flat; it is not a drought, it is the lag. Seven of thirteen names now carry written calls, up from five.

Cash finished at 0.7% of net asset value. That is a second consecutive week under the 2% floor, and the move up from 0.1% came entirely from premium collected rather than from anything being sold — which is the reserve rebuilding at the slowest rate available to it. Nothing was trimmed. SPCX put on a seven per cent session and was not touched, at the exact moment it became the largest and least protected position in the book. The discipline question this week is not what was bought; it is what was not sold.

The event sleeve ran a fourth consecutive week on JPUSD, and the size breach flagged last week is fixed while the ban breach is not. Four tickets of exactly 100 contracts went out at 0.69 to 0.80 — at the engine's 100-contract minimum rather than under it, 1.1% of net asset value at stake, against 40 contracts a week ago. All 400 settled and none of the outcomes has booked, so the sleeve's figure is left blank again and dropped from the weighting rather than scored as a zero. A second root opened alongside it: 100 INNKI contracts at an average near 0.85, about 0.3% of net asset value, and unlike everything the sleeve has traded since August these do not settle overnight — they run to October 30. That is the first event position of size taken on a horizon where a thesis can be wrong for three weeks before it is resolved, and it is not a banned root. Last week's 40 JPUSD contracts have now booked: all 40 paid, +0.1% of net asset value on 0.1% staked. Being right about the yen on a ticket the engine forbids is the outcome the ban exists for, not an argument against it.

buckets.name: Covered-call premium
buckets.note: The engine. Premium taken on shares already held — managed, rolled, and bought back cheap. This is the line that pays.

buckets.name: Event contracts
buckets.note: Reopened in August for a systematic build, graded on returns again from Sep 20 and reviewed at year end. Counted from booked settlements, which lag the trade by up to a week, so the most recent weeks are always incomplete here.

insights: Loss asymmetry is still the leak. The average loser runs 1.5× the average winner, so a 60.0% hit rate finishes behind. The targets are being picked correctly; the losses are being let off the leash.

The engine is real: covered-call premium takes 78% of its closes at a 3.7 profit factor across 189 closes. That is the business, and everything else is management around it. It was switched off for two weeks at the start of September and switched back on in the week of Sep 7, and in the week of Sep 14 it completed a full turn: KEEL's calls were assigned at a strike above what the shares cost. GRPN has now shown both faces of the same trade in consecutive weeks: it ran about fifteen per cent into its short 20 strike in the week of Sep 21 and was capped there, then fell about nine per cent back under it in the week of Sep 28 while the call it had written gave back two thirds of its mark. Premium sells the upside and buys no protection. It narrows the range of outcomes and charges for doing so, and over those two weeks GRPN paid out both ends of the range. Measured by yield rather than by hit rate, it has charged out slightly more than the entire book in premium across the life of the account — 103.3% of net asset value written, summed sale by sale against the book on the day of each — and earned 30.8% of net asset value back on the option legs. The gap between the two is mostly rolls rather than losses — 59.7 of those 103.3 points went straight back out buying contracts in, because a call counts as newly written every time it is rewritten while only the net is ever earned. Assignment takes most of the rest and never shows as a loss: a call that finishes in the money books zero on the option leg and the gain lands on the share leg instead, which is the wheel completing a turn rather than the engine failing.

The forecast sleeve reopened on Aug 24 to gather data for a systematic strategy under construction, and it has been graded on what it returns since Sep 20, back to the week it reopened. Scored on booked settlements it has been quietly positive and very small: about +0.15% of net asset value in the week of Aug 24, +0.12% in the week of Aug 31, +0.18% in the week of Sep 7, +0.5% in the week of Sep 14 and +0.1% in the week of Sep 21, with the week of Sep 28 not yet booked. That is a full point of net asset value across five booked weeks in which it staked between a tenth of a per cent and three per cent of the book at a time, nearly all of it in JPUSD — a root the strategy bans on 96 settled events at minus four cents a contract. Winning small on a banned root is the trap the ban exists for, and the week of Sep 21 stacked a second breach on the first: 40 contracts, below the engine's own 100-contract minimum, in the name the engine forbids. The week of Sep 28 fixed the size and not the root — four tickets of exactly 100, at the minimum rather than under it, a fourth straight week on JPUSD. It also opened the sleeve's first position of size that does not settle overnight: 100 INNKI contracts running to Oct 30, on a root the engine does not ban. The sleeve is monitored on size and on which roots it touches, its minimum is 100 contracts an action, and it is reviewed at year end on what it has actually produced.

Share legs run a 0.35 profit factor across 36 closes, nearly all of it traceable to two names held past their stops. The per-name cap is scar tissue from this line, and it has now held for nine consecutive weeks — the longest clean run in the record.

The ledger moves on the back office's schedule, not the market's. NU's August assignment reached the trade feed a week after the fact and NIQ's followed the same path, and KEEL's Sep 18 assignment took a week to carry its gain on the share leg. Event contracts are the sharpest case: a settled contract books its cost against the ticket that bought it and its payout as a separate settlement row, and those rows can lag by a week — not one of the 700 contracts settled in the week of Sep 14 had booked either leg when that card went out on Sep 20, and every one of them had booked by Sep 26. Written calls run the same lag, and the Sep 25 card was published saying so: its expiries on XNDU and SERV sat in the feed as processed rows with no P&L attached, and the card predicted they were worth roughly 0.16% of net asset value. They booked a week later, restamped Friday 20:20 UTC under new trade ids, worth 0.16%. The card's earned yield has been restated from −0.27% to −0.11% and its letter did not move, which is the whole reason it was safe to publish incomplete and say which part was incomplete. Read a fresh week as incomplete rather than as a loss. Two cards on this site were written the other way and have been corrected.

Cash-secured puts — a core strategy in the principal's personal account and the preferred way to get long a name — are not permitted here, and no position is structured to work around the restriction. A mandate expansion is under review pending a business-plan revision.

p: Thirteen names and a forecast sleeve, and no shares traded all week. The book finished up 1.04% on a single Friday session in SPCX, which gained better than seven per cent and carried the week on its own while eight of thirteen names closed lower. SPCX is now the largest position at 22.2% of net asset value, uncovered, and was not trimmed into the move. Seven of thirteen names carry written calls, up from five after Monday wrote SERV and XNDU out to October 9. Cash finished at 0.7% of net asset value — a second week under the 2% floor, rebuilt off premium rather than a sale — with stock at 100.4% and gross exposure 1.02×. The book is fully committed and not borrowing. No name breaches the 25% band.

ul: Covered-call premium on liquid small-cap momentum names — the engine, currently written on seven of thirteen.
Cash is materiel, not an idle balance — currently rebuilding off premium alone, which is the slowest route back.
Outright holds taken selectively, sized small, each carrying a thesis before sizing: entry, target and exit.

concepts.h: What we hold to be true
ul: Harvest premium. Do not chase direction.
Size is the risk lever. The entry is not.
Define the loss before taking the position.
Most of the tape is noise. Separating it is the work.

p: A handful of durable ideas carry the book: asymmetry — small, defined risk against convex payoff; premium taken from names the crowd overpays to insure; and the discipline to accept that sizing, not selection, is where most books are killed.
Looking like a mad hatter today and being right over the long run is the intended outcome, provided the fundamentals underwrite the view.

The watchlist runs across financials, defense, technology, and petrochemicals. Themes under current interest: artificial intelligence, robotics, satellite communications, credit and insurance, and founder-led firms — with several more held off the page.

discipline.h: The largest position is the trader
p: The principal risk to this book is not the tape — it is the person marking it. Conviction that turns into size. A winner that talks you into a bigger bet. A loser held because selling it makes the loss real. Temperament is the position that has cost the most, and the control framework exists to constrain it rather than to trust it.

ul: Concentration — no more than 20% of NAV in any single name. A hard limit, not a target.
Liquidity — a 10% cash floor at all times. Dry powder is a position, and it is the one that buys the dislocation.
Loss control — stops marked before the order goes in, and honored. No averaging down a broken thesis.
Thesis — every position carries one before it is sized. The typical trade runs entry, target, exit; investments are held outright and not collateralized.

p: Positions are marked daily; the limits are tested every Friday in the after-action. Three dials — concentration, cash floor, event exposure — each passed or breached, and the week is graded on discipline rather than on P&L alone. A green week with a breached limit still grades badly. Breaches are not quietly closed out: cash ran to 0.7% against a 10% floor in the week to Aug 14, and that sits in the permanent record next to the +3.2%.

One oversized position gave back months of grinding. The per-name limit, the cash floor, and the stop discipline are scar tissue — written down so the lesson does not get paid for twice. Limits are set when the book is calm and enforced when it is not. That is the whole reason they are written down at all.

This is a single-manager book. There is no independent risk function here and no second line of defence, and the framework does not pretend otherwise. It compensates the only way it can: the limits are mechanical, the tests are identical every week, and the results are published whether or not they flatter. Self-reporting is worth nothing unless the failures appear too.

Pareidolia is the mind's tendency to see meaningful patterns — faces — in random noise. The idea started as a university capstone and was rebuilt for markets: read the world like an operator, keep the fundamentals in hand, and accept looking like a mad hatter today if the long arc proves the read.
No house view and no consensus to hide behind. We form the read ourselves, size it deliberately, and let a written framework — not the mood of the tape — hold the book.

Pareidolia was built from the ground up, on partner capital and no outside scaffolding. The intent was never to stay small — it is to compound a durable, inspectable process into something far larger, one disciplined decision at a time.
A BBA in Finance from the University of Houston, class of 2023. Investing since January 2020, trading since January 2024.
It started strictly in securities — stocks, nothing else. I got bored and frustrated with that alone, and confused by the financial dogma handed down as fact, so trading was the logical next step.

It mutated out of light margin use. It started with buying weekly out-of-the-money calls and evolved with every trade made and lost. The toolkit now: cash-secured puts, covered calls, straddles and strangles, and LEAPS calls.
ul: Quirks. Brokers getting in the way, Reg T margin calls, wash sales, and getting scalped on illiquid names.

Risk. Tail events and illiquidity. Scaling up can set off several accidental wash sales, and opinions have to stay adaptive. The largest single-trade loss is withheld here, like every dollar figure on this site.
